knowledge_point.title: Determining Whether a Vector Lies in the Span of Given Vectors

question.:question/problem:
The vectors $\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are given below. Determine whether $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}\}$. In the affirmative case, find $x_{1}\cdot x_{2}$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{b}=x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}$.
$\mathbf{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}$
$\mathbf{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$
$\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
By the definition of span, $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}\}$ exactly when coefficients exist such that

$$
x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}=\mathbf{b}.
$$

Equating components gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-x_{1}-2x_{2} &= -3 \\ -x_{1}+2x_{2} &= 3 \\ 3x_{1}+2x_{2} &= 4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix and use elementary row operations:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & 4\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{2}\leftarrow R_{2}-\left(1\right)R_{1}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 2 & 4\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-\left(-3\right)R_{1}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & -4 & -5\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-\left(-1\right)R_{2}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-1 & -2 & -3 \\ 0 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right]
$$

Row $3$ gives $0=1$, a contradiction. No coefficients satisfy every component, so $\mathbf{b}\notin \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}\}$.

knowledge_point.title: Determining Whether a Vector Lies in the Span of Given Vectors

question.:question/problem:
The vectors $\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are given below. Determine whether $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}\}$. In the affirmative case, find $x_{1}\cdot x_{2}$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{b}=x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}$.
$\mathbf{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$
$\mathbf{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}$
$\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3 \\ -9\end{bmatrix}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
By the definition of span, $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}\}$ exactly when coefficients exist such that

$$
x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}=\mathbf{b}.
$$

Equating components gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x_{1}-x_{2} &= 3 \\ x_{1}+x_{2} &= -3 \\ x_{1}+3x_{2} &= -9\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix and use elementary row operations:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 3 & -9\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{2}\leftarrow R_{2}-\left(1\right)R_{1}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 \\ 1 & 3 & -9\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-\left(1\right)R_{1}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & 4 & -12\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-\left(2\right)R_{2}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

Back-substitution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x_{2} &= \frac{-6}{2} = -3 \\ x_{1} &= \frac{3-\left(-1\right)\left(-3\right)}{1} = 0\end{aligned}
$$

All component equations hold. Thus $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}\}$ and the coefficients are unique. Finally,

$$
x_{1}\cdot x_{2}=\left(0\right)\cdot \left(-3\right)=0.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Determining Whether a Vector Lies in the Span of Given Vectors

question.:question/problem:
The vectors $\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are given below. Determine whether $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}\}$. In the affirmative case, find $x_{1}\cdot x_{2}$ from the decomposition $\mathbf{b}=x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}$.
$\mathbf{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
$\mathbf{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}$
$\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
By the definition of span, $\mathbf{b}\in \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}\}$ exactly when coefficients exist such that

$$
x_{1}\mathbf{a}_{1}+x_{2}\mathbf{a}_{2}=\mathbf{b}.
$$

Equating components gives

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x_{1}+3x_{2} &= 4 \\ x_{1}+x_{2} &= 4 \\ 6x_{2} &= 3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Set up the augmented matrix and use elementary row operations:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 6 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{2}\leftarrow R_{2}-\left(1\right)R_{1}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

$$
R_{3}\leftarrow R_{3}-\left(-3\right)R_{2}
$$

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right]
$$

Row $3$ gives $0=3$, a contradiction. No coefficients satisfy every component, so $\mathbf{b}\notin \operatorname{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}\}$.
